query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

In this context, one of the biggest challenges is the development of structural and functional materials that can withstand the conditions inside the reactor: high temperature, high heat flux, and intense flux of high energy neutrons []. The diverter, located at the bottom of the plasma chamber, where the thermal power from the plasma is exhausted [], is one of the most challenging areas. Tungsten (W), with a high melting temperature, low sputtering rates, low neutron activation, and low tritium and deuterium retention [,], was chosen as the plasma-facing material. CuCrZr alloy was chosen as the heat sink due to its high thermal conductivity and strength. However, there is a gap between the operating temperatures of these two materials. Tungsten presents a high ductile–brittle temperature transition (DBTT) [], which requires a high-temperature operation, while CuCrZr alloy presents relatively low working temperatures (180–350 °C) [], with loss of ductility caused by irradiation embrittlement at lower temperatures and loss of mechanical strength at higher temperatures due to over-aging [,]. The main requirements for a suitable reactor wall material are good thermal conductivity, high resistance to sputtering, erosion and neutron irradiation, and the ability to withstand variations in the temperature and magnetic field. The WMoNbTaV alloy can respond to the majority of these demands. The crystalline structure of the alloy is affected by multiple strengthening effects and secondary phases, generating exceptional hardness and mechanical durability []. Ideally, one feature of an appropriate wall material would also be the lack of hydrogen trapping defects created under irradiation, leading to low retention of fusion fuel. In this study, we quantify the amount of retained hydrogen and deuterium in WMoTaNbV and compare results with those of W, the current material of choice. Deuterium is used to model tritium retention properties in order to avoid radiological hazards. Despite the differences in the masses of these hydrogen isotopes, their chemical properties are similar, and their trapping behavior in metals is comparable.
